facts.claim: "Never Been Over" was written by Darius Rucker, Lee Thomas Miller and John Osborne of Brothers Osborne.
Discogs credits Ross Copperman as producer of "Never Been Over" (track 3 on Carolyn's Boy).
Qobuz lists Ross Copperman as producer and engineer of the track, and F. Reid Shippen among the mixing, recording and engineering credits on the album.
The song runs 3:25 and is on Carolyn's Boy, released October 6, 2023 on Capitol Records Nashville.
The song directly references Rucker's recent divorce after 20 years of marriage. Garden & Gun premiered it just before the album came out.
Rucker told Garden & Gun that writing the song was very cathartic and "almost like therapy for me." He called it one of his favorite songs he has written.
Rucker told Taste of Country it was the first song he wrote about the divorce, and that it was tough to write and tough to sing.
Rucker began writing the song early in the COVID-19 pandemic. His co-writers saw it as a love song, while he saw it more as a breakup song.
The song first appeared as a solo cut. A duet re-recording with Jennifer Nettles was released in April 2024 and went to country radio on May 20, 2024.
Carolyn's Boy is Rucker's first solo album in six years. It is dedicated to his mother, Carolyn, who raised him as a single parent and died before his success.

research.lineage: Contemporary mainstream Nashville country: a personal ballad from Rucker, who rose with Hootie & the Blowfish and later became a country solo artist.

draft:
The trick of **Never Been Over** is that the whole song is built from denials. The chorus runs through every breakup scene a country song could reach for: friends divided, records divided, walls going up, letters going into the fire, taillights shrinking down the road. This couple, the narrator insists, has never been any of it. Then the title phrase lands, "But we've never been over," and it sounds like a vow and a wish at the same time.

Who's singing it changes everything. Darius Rucker wrote the song with Lee Thomas Miller and John Osborne of Brothers Osborne, starting early in the pandemic, and it was the first thing he wrote about his divorce after 20 years of marriage. His co-writers heard a love song. He heard a breakup song. Both readings live in the lyric, and the song never makes you pick one. The verses list what this pair has come through: sunny days and straight-line wind, blue lights on back roads, dead quiet and rockstar loud. The pride in that list is real. So is the dread under it. The second verse slips in a line the rest of the song can't take back: "Knowing that day will come." Later the bridge admits why they're still standing: "That we don't know how to run." That isn't quite devotion. It's love that has outlasted the knowledge of how to leave, and Rucker lets the tenderness and the trap sit side by side.

The arrangement stays easy so the words can do the hurting. Brushed drums keep a steady beat, a walking bass line moves underneath, an acoustic guitar strums, and steel guitar holds long, sustained notes. The groove is relaxed. Ross Copperman's production is clean, with a natural room sound and nothing pushed to the front except the voice. Rucker sings conversationally, slightly raspy in the middle of his range, with a second voice blended in close harmony. It's contemporary Nashville through and through, polished and unhurried, and that plainness suits an artist who rose with Hootie & the Blowfish before building a country solo career. He doesn't oversell a single line.

Rucker called the writing "almost like therapy for me" and said the song was tough to sing. The structure shows the strain. The chorus comes around three times, each pass a little harder to believe, and at the end the setup line repeats and stalls before the payoff finally arrives, as if the singer needs one more breath before saying it.

It's a love song sung by someone who already knows how the story ends, and the gap between what the words swear and what the singer knows is the thing that keeps pulling you back.
